name: Tera
confidence_why: The quoted passage has not been checked against the cited source.
catalog_citation: Tench, Paul. 2007. Tera. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 37(2): 227-234. doi:10.1017/S0025100307002952 (Illustrations of the IPA; open-access Cambridge Core PDF). Corroborated by Newman, Paul. 1964. A word list of Tera. Journal of West African Languages 1(2): 33-50 (free JWAL back-issue scan, scan of pp. 33-37).
catalog_locator: Tench 2007: p. 232, section 'Tone' (page 232, re-extracted with); Newman 1964: p. 35, sec. 4 and fn. 7 (scan).
catalog_quote: Tench 2007: 232, 'Tone': "The tone system of Tera has not been described before. What follows is a preliminary analysis of mono- and disyllabic lexical items; no attempt has yet been made to investigate tone in discourse. Tone is not generally marked in the new orthography, since no contrasts exist in ‘minimal trios’ and those in ‘minimal pairs’ can be distinguished in context. ... There are three contrasting level tones: high (H [´]), mid (M, unmarked) and low (L [`]). There appear to be no contour tones, even in syllables with long and diphthongal vowels. ... Disyllabic words display the following seven patterns; there appear to be no sequences of HL or LH. Mid tone is partially assimilated to a neighbouring H or L, producing either mid-high or mid-low. [HH, HM, MH, MM, ML, LM, LL] ... In most cases there seems to be some sort of interaction between voicing and tone with voiced obstruents favouring L tone while voiceless obstruents and implosives can be followed by any tone, but there is not enough evidence for a categorical statement at this point." || Newman 1964: 35, sec. 4: "Tera has three basic tones[fn.7]: high [´], mid (unmarked in this paper) and low [`]. What appear as rising and falling tones can in all cases be analysed as a sequence of two level tones." fn. 7: "Three tonemes are necessary and sufficient for marking lexical items. I have not yet worked out the more complex tonal pattern of longer utterances."
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tera is described as a lexical tone language with three level tones (H, M, L) on every syllable; neither Tench 2007 nor Newman 1964 says anything about word stress or accent, so no stress placement rule is on record in the accessible primary descriptions.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any accessible source.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tone notes only: no HL/LH on disyllables; mid tone partially assimilates to neighbouring H or L; possible voicing-tone interaction (voiced obstruents favour L).
new_statements.domain_note: Both descriptions treat isolated lexical items (mono- and disyllables); Tench explicitly has not analysed tone in discourse, Newman fn.7 likewise for longer utterances. Silence on stress is silence, not a claim that stress is absent.
new_statements.identity_note: Tench 2007 describes the 'standard' Tera of radio news, from speakers of Deba, Hinna, Difa, Zambuk and Lubo (Gombe State); Newman 1964/1970 are based on one speaker from Wuyo (eastern Tera area). Same language, tera1251; Newman notes Tera and Pidlimdi (Hinna) form one dialect cluster.

new_statements.quote: Chapter 6 turns to Tera, a Chadic language of northern Nigeria whose word phonology is organized differently again, around tone and mora-based syllable structure rather than stress and feet. [...] The final case study of Tera represented in Chapter 6 is the most radical in terms of its difference from English. Tera is a Chadic language that lacks feet in the stress-based sense, and its word phonology is organized around the distinction between heavy and light syllables and the use of lexical tone. [...] In this chapter, Tench constructs system networks to account for tone patterns on lexical items, for vowels in light and heavy syllables, for word-initial and word-final consonants, and for syllable-final consonants in word-medial positions.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's existing statement (Tench 2007 JIPA p.232: three level tones H/M/L, no statement on stress; Newman 1964 p.35: three basic tones). Adds, at second hand from Tench 2024 ch. 6, an explicit statement about stress: Tera 'lacks feet in the stress-based sense' and its word phonology is organized 'around tone and mora-based syllable structure rather than stress and feet'. No placement is asserted, so nothing contradicts the catalog; it upgrades 'no stress statement' to 'source says word phonology is not stress-based'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Per the reviewers' summary of Tench (2024) ch. 6, Tera word phonology is built on lexical tone and a heavy/light (moraic) syllable distinction, not on stress or stress-based feet; i.e. Tera is a tone language with no stress-foot organization at word level. No stress placement rule is given because stress is said not to be the organizing principle.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none mentioned (the work denies stress-based feet for Tera).
new_statements.exceptions: none. The review is a secondary source paraphrasing Tench's 2024 monograph (University of Toronto Press ed., xii+189 pp., ISBN 978-1-4875-6652-4); it gives no Tera data, tone values or page numbers within ch. 6 beyond the general characterization.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources concern Tera (Nyimatli) of Gombe State, northern Nigeria, as described by Paul Tench (2007, 2024) and Paul Newman (1964, 1970); the review names no particular dialect.
